summary: The Democratic Republic of the Congo lies in central Africa, is the second-largest country in Africa by area, has the Congo River and vast rainforests and abundant mineral resources, but has long been troubled by conflict.

ranking.name: Other Christian denominations (including Pentecostal and revival churches)
ranking.description: This category includes Pentecostal churches, revival churches and various indigenous independent churches, which grew rapidly in the late Mobutu regime of the 1990s and during the two Congo wars of 1996–2003. War and economic collapse led many people to turn to new churches emphasizing miracles, healing and prosperity theology, and 'revival churches' can be seen everywhere on the streets of Kinshasa, making this category the largest Christian group.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: Catholicism was first introduced at the end of the 15th century when the Portuguese reached the Kingdom of Kongo, and the king of Kongo was baptized in 1491, but it later declined. In the late 19th century King Leopold II of Belgium established the Congo Free State (1885–1908), which became the Belgian Congo after 1908, and the Catholic Church, with the support of the colonial government, controlled most of education and health care. The Catholic Church played an important political role both during the Mobutu dictatorship and in the protests against Kabila's extension of his term in 2016–2018.

ranking.name: Protestantism
ranking.description: Protestantism was introduced to the lower Congo River in 1878 by English Baptist missionaries, after which American, British and Swedish missions established churches and schools in various places. In 1970 the Mobutu government merged the Protestant denominations into the 'Church of Christ in Congo', which became an officially recognized organization alongside the Catholic Church. Protestantism is especially strong in the east and the Kongo Central area.

ranking.name: Kimbanguist Church
ranking.description: The Kimbanguist Church was founded by Simon Kimbangu, who began preaching in the Lower Congo area of the Belgian Congo in 1921 and attracted large numbers of followers with miraculous healings. The Belgian colonial authorities regarded him as a threat and arrested him the same year and sentenced him to death (later commuted to life imprisonment); he spent 30 years in prison and died in 1951. In 1959 the Kimbanguist Church was granted legal status, and it is one of the largest indigenous Christian churches in Africa.

ranking.name: Islam
ranking.description: Islam was introduced to the east in the 19th century by Arab and Swahili slave traders from East Africa, the most famous being the trader Tippu Tip, who built a trading network in eastern Congo. In 1892–1894 war broke out between the Congo Free State and the Arab-Swahili forces, and the expansion of Islam was checked; today Muslims make up only about 1%, mainly in the eastern provinces of Kisangani and Maniema.

religion.background: Before colonization the Congo region had the traditional beliefs of many peoples, centered on ancestor and nature-spirit worship. At the end of the 15th century the Portuguese brought Catholicism to the Kingdom of Kongo, but the influence was mainly limited to the coast. In the late 19th century King Leopold II of Belgium's Congo Free State imposed a brutal rubber-collection system that caused millions of deaths, while Catholic and Protestant missionaries entered the interior. In the colonial period the churches controlled education and health care, and Kimbangu's movement of 1921 represented an African-led religious and political awakening. After independence in 1960, Christianity became the faith of the great majority, and new churches grew rapidly amid the turmoil of war.

language.official: French is the official language; Lingala, Swahili, Kikongo and Tshiluba are national languages.

ranking.name: Swahili
ranking.description: Swahili originated in the fusion of Bantu and Arabic on the East African coast and spread to eastern Congo in the 19th century as Arab and Swahili traders from East Africa penetrated inland; during the Belgian colonial period it was also used as an administrative and army language in the east. Today it is the lingua franca of the east, in Katanga and the Kivus, and is one of the four national languages of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, with the most speakers.

ranking.name: Lingala
ranking.description: Lingala originates from the Bangala language of the middle Congo River and was adopted by the army and river transport in the late 19th century during the Belgian colonial period, spreading with the Force Publique and river traders. Much of the popular music of the capital Kinshasa (such as rumba and soukous) is sung in Lingala, which has made it widely popular across the country and in neighboring countries, and it is the main lingua franca of the west and the capital.

ranking.name: Tshiluba
ranking.description: Tshiluba is the language of the Luba people of the Kasai region of the center-south, and the Luba Kingdom was an important state in central Africa in the 16th–19th centuries. During the Belgian colonial period Tshiluba was used as the language of education and administration in the Kasai region; today it is the lingua franca of provinces such as East Kasai and West Kasai and is one of the four national languages.

ranking.name: Kikongo
ranking.description: Kikongo is the language of the Kongo people of the Lower Congo region in the west, an area that was once part of the Kingdom of Kongo of the 14th–19th centuries. Because the Kongo are distributed across the Democratic Republic of the Congo, the Republic of the Congo and Angola, Kikongo is a cross-border language; in the colonial period a simplified Kituba became popular in the railways and commerce and became the lingua franca of the west.

ranking.name: French
ranking.description: French arrived with the colonial rule of the Congo Free State in 1885 and the Belgian Congo in 1908; in the colonial period it was the language of administration and higher education, and it remained the official language after independence in 1960. The Democratic Republic of the Congo is one of the countries with the most French speakers in the world, but because the four national languages are mostly used in daily life, very few have French as their mother tongue.

language.history: The Democratic Republic of the Congo has more than 200 languages, mostly of the Bantu family. In the Belgian colonial period of the late 19th century, in order to administer the vast territory, the colonial authorities chose four regional lingua francas: Kikongo in the west, Lingala in the capital and the north, Tshiluba in the center-south and Swahili in the east, used alongside French. After independence in 1960, French was the official language and the four lingua francas became national languages. From 1971 to 1997 Mobutu pursued the 'authenticité' campaign, emphasizing indigenous culture, but French remained the main language of national administration and education.

ranking.name: Moambe (palm nut chicken)
ranking.description: Chicken is stewed in a thick sauce made by cooking palm fruit, with garlic, onion and chili, with a rich sauce, often served with rice or fufu.
ranking.history: Palm nut chicken is regarded as the national dish of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and 'moambe' in Lingala refers to the sauce of palm fruit. The oil palm is a plant native to the tropical rainforest of the Congo basin, and in the colonial period the Belgians planted oil palms on a large scale in the Congo; in 1911 Lever Brothers, the forerunner of Britain's Unilever, obtained large oil palm concessions in the Congo. The dish also spread to Belgium with Belgian colonization and became a signature dish of local African restaurants.

ranking.name: Fufu
ranking.description: Cassava flour or maize flour is stirred with hot water into an elastic dough-like staple, with a sticky, slippery texture, pinched into small balls by hand and dipped in stews or sauces.
ranking.history: Cassava is native to South America and was brought by the Portuguese to the coast of the Kingdom of Kongo in the 16th century, quickly becoming a staple because it is drought-tolerant and high-yielding; the Democratic Republic of the Congo is today one of the world's largest producers of cassava. Fufu is the most common staple in the west and the capital, while in the east more 'ugali' made from maize is eaten. It is the basic meal eaten daily in almost every Congolese household.

ranking.name: Pondu (cassava leaf stew)
ranking.description: Cassava leaves are pounded and stewed for a long time with palm oil, onion, garlic and dried fish, with a thick texture, often eaten with fufu or rice.
ranking.history: Cassava leaf stew is called 'pondu' in Lingala and is very common in the Congo basin; cassava leaves are rich in protein and an important source of nutrition. Because cassava is grown in large quantities in the Congo, the leaves are cheap and easy to get and have become the everyday food of poor families. It is similar to the 'saka-saka' of the neighboring Republic of the Congo, reflecting the food culture shared on both banks of the Congo River.

ranking.name: Liboke
ranking.description: Fish or meat with onion, tomato and chili is wrapped in banana (plantain) leaves and roasted over charcoal, keeping the original flavor of the ingredients, with the fresh fragrance of the leaves.
ranking.history: Liboke is a traditional cooking method of the Congo basin, and 'liboke' means 'package' in Lingala. The Congo River is the world's second-largest river and rich in fish of all kinds, and fishermen traditionally wrap fish in banana leaves and roast them directly over charcoal. Today liboke is a common dish at restaurants and family gatherings in Kinshasa, with grilled fish the most common.

ranking.name: Chikwangue (cassava sticks)
ranking.description: Cassava is soaked in water to ferment and pounded into a paste, wrapped in banana or bamboo leaves into long sticks and steamed, with a firm, elastic texture and a slight sourness.
ranking.history: Chikwangue is a traditional staple of the Congo basin, and the method of fermenting, wrapping and steaming removes the cyanide from cassava and lets the food keep for days to weeks. This method makes chikwangue an ideal dry ration for long journeys and river voyages. Today stalls selling chikwangue can be seen everywhere in the markets and streets of Kinshasa, often eaten with grilled fish or grilled meat.
